questions.q: What is the ITIL 4 purpose of the incident management practice?
options: To approve or reject proposed changes to the IT environment
To find the root cause of every service disruption before restoring service
To track the full lifecycle of every physical and digital asset
To minimize the negative impact of incidents by restoring normal service operation as quickly as possible
questions.explain: Incident management exists to restore service fast — not to diagnose why it broke.

questions.q: A warehouse-wide outage affects hundreds of workers and is losing the business money every minute. Which factor makes this incident high priority?
options: The incident cannot be prioritized until its root cause is known
Priority only depends on which team reported it
High urgency, because it needs fixing very quickly
Low impact, because only one service is affected
questions.explain: Priority comes from impact (how much damage) combined with urgency (how fast it must be fixed); a business-wide, money-bleeding outage scores high on both.

questions.q: What distinguishes swarming from traditional tiered escalation?
options: Tiered escalation is only used for major incidents
Swarming always takes longer than tiered escalation
Tiered escalation passes an incident up one level at a time; swarming pulls multiple resolvers together at once
Swarming is a type of change, not a resolution model for incidents
questions.explain: ITIL 4 describes both models: sequential handoffs between tiers, or multiple people working the incident together from the start.

questions.q: Why does a major incident get its own separate, faster-moving process?
options: Because the normal queue-and-prioritize flow is too slow when impact and visibility are already extremely high
Because only problem management can handle major incidents
Because major incidents don't need to be logged
Because major incidents are always caused by failed changes
questions.explain: A major incident runs under a dedicated, expedited process with its own coordinator and more frequent stakeholder communication.

questions.q: A team restores a crashed service by restarting it, with no idea yet why it crashed. Per ITIL 4, has incident management succeeded?
options: No — the incident cannot close until the root cause is identified
No — only a workaround documented in problem management counts as a resolution
Yes, but only if the restart also prevents a recurrence
Yes — restoring normal service operation is the goal, regardless of whether the root cause is known
questions.explain: Incident management's job is restoration; root cause analysis is explicitly the responsibility of problem management, not incident management.
